verdict: ROOT CAUSE FOUND. Normal alignment pulled the SHORTEST axis from 3.45cm to 1.23cm and left the LONGEST at 8.49->8.47cm, unchanged. We converted roughly isotropic blobs into wide flat pancakes: geometrically ideal, photometrically a smear. 57% of visible gaussians project wider than 5px and a gravel stone is about 5px, so one gaussian covers the thing it is meant to depict. This is why geometry metrics rose while the image did not - wall thickness, shortest-axis angle and floater distance ALL measure the thin direction, and NOTHING measured the longest axis. It also explains the capacity result: extra primitives never got smaller, so they had nothing new to encode. geometry_regularization - which exists in this repo with exactly the needed knobs - was {enabled: false} in every config of this campaign, and MCMC relocates instead of splitting, so unlike classic 3DGS nothing capped growth. The best PSNR in this whole log (20.41, gs2 scale-tail) is the one run that used it.

verdict: BACKFIRED, AND THE AUDIT IS WHY WE KNOW. verdict: SHARP BUT WRONG - AND THIS IS WHY ENERGY ALONE IS NOT A GATE. Energy leapt 0.199 -> 0.829, four times any other arm, and the crop does show real structure appearing where there had been flat beige: wall courses, mortar lines, shrubs, poppies. But PSNR fell to 13.36, SSIM to 0.3631, LPIPS did not move (0.5387 -> 0.5397), and the rendered gravel is oversized smooth pebbles rather than the fine angular chips in the photo. Adding a second axis settles it: gradient AGREEMENT (correlation between the render's gradient map and the photo's) is 0.180, the LOWEST of every model measured, below even the blurred ones. Most of that new high-frequency energy is uncorrelated with the scene - invented, not recovered. Recorded as a negative result: the mechanism proves the model CAN express detail, which is progress, but it does not prove the detail is right.

SECOND SHARPNESS AXIS ADDED AFTER G3 EXPOSED THE FIRST ONE'S BLIND SPOT. Energy cannot tell sharp from noisy - speckle scores as well as resolution. Correlation of the two gradient maps separates them: blur attenuates gradients but leaves them where the real edges are (low energy, moderate agreement); noise scores high energy and ~0 agreement; only detail that is present AND correct scores high on both. Caveat recorded honestly - blurred models get agreement cheaply because a blurred edge is still at the edge, so the metric is biased in their favour and a low absolute value for a sharp model is not automatically damning. On this ranking NO model is close to usable, and the campaign's question splits in two: 'can it express detail' (solved by the footprint clamp) and 'can it determine the CORRECT detail' (open, and the single-view overfit is the experiment that decides whether pose is to blame).

legacy_unlabeled_values: points3D 643509; observations 2368262; track 3.68; mean reprojection 1.574 px; valid matches 48.6%
verdict: FIRST BA STAGE EVER RUN ON UKGS. Installed the three runtime dependencies the pipeline needed and that this machine lacked (pycolmap 4.1.1 from a cp312 win_amd64 wheel, lightglue and hloc from the exact commits in upstream/rig_ba.lock.json); the lock verification passes. IMPORTANT READING: COLMAP's own 1.574 px is NOT comparable to the 3.19 px measured by tools/pose_reprojection_audit.py, and the gap between them is informative rather than contradictory. Triangulation OPTIMISES the 3D points to fit the observations given the poses, so pose error is absorbed into point positions; the audit uses LiDAR-measured geometry that cannot move, so it exposes error the triangulation hides. Together they say the cameras agree with EACH OTHER to ~1.6 px but disagree with the LIDAR by ~3.2 px, which splits the problem: trajectory error is reachable by BA, camera-to-LiDAR extrinsic error is not.

REJECTED BY THE SCALE GATE, CORRECTLY - AND THE REJECTION IS THE USEFUL PART. Reprojection improved 34.9%, clearing the 30% gate and landing at 1.045 px, better than gs2 reached after its own BA (1.08). Ceres converged in 82 iterations, the rig baseline held to 1e-14, and camera intrinsics did not move. But median pair distance went 7.133 m -> 7.307 m: a 2.44% scale drift against a 0.5% limit, so candidate_accepted=false and the published model is 'before' - the poses on disk are untouched. Scale is not a free parameter here: it comes from LiDAR SLAM, which measures range directly, so drifting off it is an error, not a recovery, and on a survey product a 2.4% error misreports every distance. Diagnosis: with 2.37M observations pulling on reprojection, a 0.05 m per-camera POS prior is too weak to anchor the gauge. Next: sweep the prior tighter (0.02/0.01/0.005). The two possible outcomes are both worth having - if a tight prior keeps most of the 35%, the trajectory was genuinely improvable; if the gain vanishes as the prior tightens, then the apparent improvement WAS the scale drift and the residual 3.19 px against LiDAR is extrinsic calibration, which BA cannot fix.

BA ACCEPTED. Tightening the POS prior from 0.05 m to 0.01 m cut scale drift from 2.44% to 0.18% while the reprojection gain held at -34.7%, so all gates pass and the published model is 'after'. The gain surviving unchanged across a 5x prior range is the important part: had the 35% been gauge drift in disguise, it would have collapsed as the prior tightened. It did not, so the trajectory correction is real. Final: reprojection p50 1.604 -> 1.047 px, better than gs2 reached after its own BA (1.08).

legacy_unlabeled_values: 3 cm subtends 7.8 px at 3 m, 4.7 px at 5 m, 2.3 px at 10 m (fl=778 px/rad)
verdict: CORRECTION TO MY OWN CONCLUSION, AND TO SEVERAL NUMBERS I HAVE BEEN QUOTING. The operator points out that this LiDAR is accurate to 2-3 cm and degrades at oblique incidence, so it is a reference for PLANES rather than a per-point metric truth. That invalidates the inference I drew from the patch audit. The audit lifts a patch to 3D THROUGH the LiDAR range, so a 3 cm depth error displaces the reprojection by 4.7 px at 5 m - the same magnitude as the 3-8 px offsets I measured. The measurement therefore cannot separate 'camera-to-LiDAR extrinsic error' from 'LiDAR range noise', and my verdict naming the extrinsic as the cause went beyond the evidence. What survives unaffected is the BEFORE/AFTER comparison in the BA carry-over audit: whatever the noise floor is, it is identical in both runs, so 'the BA gain does not reach the LiDAR frame' still holds. A structure test now distinguishes the two - a rigid extrinsic fault produces a COMMON shift within each frame and consistent direction across frames, while range noise scatters per point. SECOND CORRECTION, unprompted: the floater criterion is also built on this cloud. The >0.3 m thresholds sit far above a 2-3 cm noise floor and remain sound, but the d_perp MEDIANS I have been reporting and comparing (1-2 cm) are AT OR BELOW that floor, so those particular figures carry less precision than my earlier reports implied. Threshold counts: trustworthy. Median distances at centimetre scale: not resolvable by this instrument. THIRD CONSEQUENCE, now under test as phase 12: the pipeline uses the LiDAR two ways that this accuracy argument treats very differently - lidar_range_weight supervises per-pixel depth against exactly the noisy per-point measurement, giving neighbouring pixels mutually inconsistent targets, while lidar_normal_alignment fits planes through many points and averages that noise away. V2 (range off, normals kept) versus V1 (the reverse) tests which half carries the benefit; V4 already showed that removing BOTH is worse, so the question is which one, not whether.

legacy_unlabeled_values: within-frame consistency 0.43; left common shift (-0.29,-0.83) px scatter 2.70; right (-0.03,-0.58) px scatter 2.97
verdict: MY OWN PROPOSED FIX, REFUTED BEFORE I BUILT IT. Last entry I named a 6-DoF camera-to-LiDAR extrinsic solve as the next step. A rigid extrinsic fault must produce per-frame offset vectors that all point the same way, so their average is large and their scatter small. Measured: the average is UNDER 1 px for both cameras (left -0.29,-0.83; right -0.03,-0.58) while frame-to-frame scatter is 2.70 and 2.97 px - the opposite pattern. A 6-DoF solve could therefore recover well under a pixel and is not worth writing. Running this before implementing saved building the wrong thing, which is the second time in this campaign that a structure check has caught a plausible conclusion (the first being G1's scale audit). WHAT THE NUMBERS DO SAY: the error is dominated by per-frame variation, and within-frame consistency of 0.43 means it is neither rigid nor pure per-point white noise - it is locally correlated. That matches the operator's assessment exactly: 2-3 cm of LiDAR error subtends 4.7-7.8 px at 3-5 m, which covers the 2.7-3.0 px scatter, and registration error in a cloud is correlated across neighbouring points rather than independent, which produces exactly the partial within-frame consistency observed. CONCLUSION: the residual is the LiDAR's own accuracy limit, not a calibratable systematic fault. BA already showed it cannot help (-34.7% on its own residual, +2.0% on the LiDAR-relative one). Pose and calibration are now both closed as directions. The productive move is not to fix the LiDAR but to change how much the training trusts it per point - phase 12, V2 vs V1.

verdict: THE PAIR SETTLES WHICH LIDAR USE CARRIES THE BENEFIT, AND CORRECTS MY DRIVER'S OWN VERDICT. Against both-terms-on (energy 0.199): dropping range costs 0.021, dropping normals costs 0.048, dropping both costs 0.067 - almost exactly additive, so the two terms contribute independently and BOTH are net positive, with the plane term worth about 2.3x the depth term. The operator's framing is confirmed in the sense that matters - this LiDAR earns its keep as a plane reference - but not in the stronger form that per-point depth is harmful.

A PATTERN THAT HAS BEEN IN THE DATA ALL ALONG AND THAT I RANKED PAST. Sorting every arm by gradient agreement - structural correlation with the photograph - the single best model is S0, the ONLY configuration that runs no densification at all. Every arm that grows new Gaussians scores lower, without exception, and the more aggressively an arm adds or reshapes them the further it falls (G3, which shrank splats hardest, is last at 0.180). I did not see this earlier because I was ranking on energy and PSNR, and neither can see it. It suggests a hypothesis nothing has yet tested: densification itself degrades structural fidelity, because births are placed by an error heuristic and high image error does not mean real structure is present - so new Gaussians add energy without adding correlation. FALSIFIABLE AS FOLLOWS: take S0's configuration and enable ONLY densification. If agreement falls, the mechanism is confirmed; if it holds, then S0's advantage comes from something else it differs in (count, initialisation) and this reading is wrong. Design the test before believing the pattern - this campaign has twice been saved by doing that (G1's scale audit, the extrinsic structure test).

legacy_unlabeled_values: map correlation 0.189; top-decile overlap 22.0%; photo texture at disagreements: error-only 0.037 vs structure-only 0.15-0.19
verdict: WHY DENSIFICATION HURTS, MEASURED. This test was designed to KILL the follow-up idea before implementing it - if the current error map and a structure-aware one selected the same pixels, swapping them could not move where Gaussians are born and the idea was dead. They do not: correlation 0.189 and only 22% overlap in the top decile that densification actually acts on. And the disagreement has a direction. Pixels the CURRENT criterion prioritises but the structure-aware one does not carry mean photo gradient 0.037; pixels the structure-aware one picks instead carry 0.15-0.19, roughly FOUR TIMES the texture. So densification is spending capacity where the photograph has almost nothing to show - exactly what occlusion, specularity and exposure mismatch produce - and skipping the places that hold real detail. Combined with D1 this closes a full causal chain, each link measured under a single variable: births degrade agreement (D1), because they are placed by image error, and image error points at low-texture regions (this test). PROPOSED, not yet built: error map photo_gradient * (1 - local_agreement), which targets where the photo has structure the render is not following. Third time this campaign that a pre-registered falsification test decided whether to build something - the first two (G1's scale audit, the extrinsic structure test) both said no, this one says yes.

verdict: LADDER COMPLETE - DENSITY IS THE MAIN LEVER BUT DOES NOT CLOSE THE GAP ALONE. Integrated: the comparison renderer merges the dome onto every 'ours' snapshot (sky-excluded metrics untouched), and the same merge serves exports. Product path: this bake is v1; a train-time refinement (frozen positions, optimized colours) can follow once the trainer grows parameter freezing. verdict: THE USER CALLED IT: the poison segment is a TIME problem, and it is salvageable frame by frame. The measured LAS shift of every fast frame aligns with the pixel displacement of sliding that camera along ITS OWN trajectory - a 1-DoF error - and the left/right cameras vote independently, consistent with their visibly independent exposures. Because dt varies frame to frame (SLAM trajectory jitter under high angular velocity, not a fixed offset), the correction is per-frame: dt_i solved from the shift peak against a numeric d(pixel)/dt, median-smoothed along each camera's timeline, poses re-interpolated between manifest neighbours at t_i+dt_i. Slow frames keep dt=0 - they already sit at the audit floor, which is why the error only ever showed on the fast close passes. The solver runs on all 886 images behind the same fail-closed gate as every pose method before it (every decile <=4px or nothing is written). If the gate passes, q8 trains on ALL 796 train images with time-corrected poses, and q7 (BA+exclusion, in flight) becomes the reference q8 must beat to prove salvage > deletion. This also explains why rig-rigid methods failed: left and right sit at different trajectory times, so no single rig pose exists during fast motion.
